intro.html: These are words of courtrooms and consciences. Two describe responsibility and blame (accountable, culpable). Five mean clearing someone of blame, each in its own way (exculpate, exonerate, acquit, absolve, vindicate). Condone means letting wrongdoing slide, punitive describes punishment, and clemency is mercy.
Listen for the Latin: culpa = fault (culpable, exculpate); onus = burden (exonerate: the burden of blame taken off); poena = punishment (punitive, like punish).

words.def: responsible for your actions and expected to explain them
words.ex: As class treasurer, Maya was {accountable} for every dollar of the trip fund.
words.ctx: The new rules hold each driver {accountable}: if a package arrives damaged, the driver who carried it must explain what happened.

mn.cue: ACCOUNT-ABLE: able to give an ACCOUNT
mn.text: Maya, the class treasurer, can show where every dollar of the trip money went, down to the last receipt. She is {accountable}.

scene.alt: A student treasurer proudly shows her notebook of receipts to her teacher.

words.ex: The muddy paw prints showed that the dog was {culpable}.
words.ctx: The report found the builder {culpable}: he had known the beams were cracked and had covered them with paint instead of replacing them.
words.etym: From Latin culpabilis, “blameworthy,” from culpa (fault, blame).

mn.cue: CULP-able: the CULPRIT is to blame
mn.text: Muddy paw prints lead straight from the kitchen to the dog’s bed. The dog is the culprit: he is {culpable}.

scene.alt: A woman points at a guilty-looking dog sitting on its bed beside a trail of muddy paw prints.

words.def: to show that someone is not guilty
words.ex: The video from the hallway camera {exculpated} Ivy: it showed the cat knocking over the vase.
words.ctx: New letters found in the archive {exculpate} the old mayor; they show that he had warned the council about the dam years before it broke.
words.etym: From Medieval Latin exculpare, “to free from blame”: ex (out of) + culpa (blame).

mn.text: The camera shows the cat, not Ivy, knocking over the vase. The video takes the blame right out of Ivy’s hands: it {exculpates} her.

scene.alt: A boy holds up a camera that shows the cat broke the vase, and his sister cheers.

words.ex: When the real thief confessed, the police {exonerated} the gardener.
words.ctx: After ten years in prison, the man was {exonerated} by new tests that proved someone else had committed the crime.
words.etym: From Latin exonerare, “to unload, free from a burden”: ex (off) + onus (burden).

mn.cue: EX-ONUS: the load of blame lifted OFF
mn.text: When the real thief is caught, the heavy sack of blame falls off Jamal’s shoulders. He is {exonerated}.

scene.alt: A relieved man cheers as a heavy sack labeled blame falls away from him.

words.def: to declare someone not guilty in a court
words.ex: The jury {acquitted} the baker of stealing the prize-winning pie.
words.ctx: Although the newspapers had already called her guilty, the jury {acquitted} her after one hour, finding that the evidence proved nothing.
words.note: Acquit is a court word: a jury or judge acquits. Its opposite is convict.

mn.cue: AC-QUIT: you can QUIT worrying: not guilty!
mn.text: The jury foreman stands and reads, “Not guilty!” Rosa can quit worrying: the court has {acquitted} her.

scene.alt: In a courtroom, a juror reads “not guilty” and the young woman on trial cheers.

words.def: to free someone from guilt, blame or a duty
words.ex: Grandma {absolved} Pip of the broken teacup: “Accidents happen.”
words.ctx: The team’s apology did not {absolve} it of responsibility; the club still had to pay to repair the field it had damaged.
words.etym: From Latin absolvere, “to set free, loosen”: ab (from) + solvere (to loosen).

mn.text: Pip breaks Grandma’s teacup and expects a scolding, but she hugs him: “Accidents happen. You’re forgiven.” She {absolves} him.

scene.alt: A grandmother hugs her grandson and forgives him for breaking a teacup.

words.def: to clear from blame or doubt; to prove right
words.ex: When the old well gushed water, Sami felt {vindicated}.
words.ctx: For years critics mocked her theory, but the new fossils {vindicated} her: the bird’s ancestors really had walked on two legs.
words.etym: From Latin vindicare, “to claim, set free, defend.”
words.note: Vindicate has nothing to do with revenge; that is vindictive.

mn.cue: VIN = WIN: proved RIGHT at last
mn.text: Everyone laughed at Sami for saying the old well still had water, until it gushed. He wins: the gushing well {vindicates} him.

scene.alt: A boy cheers as an old well he believed in gushes water, while a doubter stares.

words.ex: The school does not {condone} copying homework.
words.ctx: By laughing along instead of stopping the teasing, the counselor seemed to {condone} it, and the campers took it as permission to continue.
words.etym: From Latin condonare, “to give up, forgive”: con + donare (to give).
words.note: Condone is nearly the opposite of condemn: to condone wrongdoing is to let it pass.

mn.cue: CON-DONE: “Eh, it’s DONE all the time”
mn.text: Pip peeks at the answer sheet, and the substitute just shrugs: “Eh, it’s done all the time.” By shrugging it off, he {condones} the cheating.

scene.alt: A boy peeks at an answer sheet while the substitute teacher just shrugs.

words.ex: A five-hundred-dollar fine for one overdue library book would be {punitive}.
words.ctx: The coach insisted the extra laps were not {punitive} but practical: the team simply needed to get in better shape before the season.
words.etym: From Medieval Latin punitivus, from Latin punire, “to punish.”

mn.text: The librarian posts a sign: one late book, a five-hundred-dollar fine! A fine like that is not a reminder; it is {punitive}.

scene.alt: A stern librarian points to a sign announcing a huge fine as a boy with a late book looks shocked.

words.ex: The queen showed {clemency} to the hungry boy who had taken a loaf of bread.
words.ctx: The judge could have given the maximum sentence, but she granted {clemency} because the young man had confessed and repaid every dollar.

mn.text: Instead of punishing the hungry boy who took a loaf of bread, the queen hands him a basket of clementines. She shows {clemency}.

scene.alt: A kind queen gives a basket of fruit to a hungry boy holding a loaf of bread.

head: clearing word
how
rows: evidence shows someone is not to blame
frees from guilt, blame or a duty; forgives

after.html: Two famous mix-ups: condone (to overlook wrongdoing) is nearly the opposite of condemn (to declare it wrong); and vindicate (to prove right) has nothing to do with vindictive (seeking revenge).

items.q: The principal said, “We do not condone cheating.” She means the school…
choices: does not accept or overlook it
items.why: To condone is to accept or overlook wrongdoing. Not condoning cheating means refusing to let it pass.

choices: The test results vindicated her claim that the water was safe.
He was so vindicated that he plotted revenge for years.
The vindicate villain swore to get even.
She vindicated her brother by breaking his toy on purpose.
items.why: To vindicate is to prove right or clear of blame. Seeking revenge is vindictive.

items.q: Which word has a Latin root meaning “burden”?
items.why: Exonerate: ex (off) + onus (burden). Exculpate has culpa (fault).

items.q: True or false: if you are culpable, you deserve the blame.
items.why: True. Culpable comes from Latin culpa, “fault.”
